candidate_text:
HEADLINE FINDING
The morning shoe battle and the kitchen chase are not stubbornness but rage called out by daily restraint, kept alive by a household that both rewards the rage by finishing the task and answers all his crying with cuddling, inside a schedule that is nowhere fixed.

STOP DOING
- Stop finishing the shoes for him once he screams and throws them. Withdraw attention entirely and let the rage burn itself out unattended.
- Stop picking him up and cuddling him each time he cries in the morning; this stroking is building an over-conditioned dependence on being soothed by contact.
- Stop answering crying, whether at the counter or at bedtime, with holding and cuddling. Handle him objectively instead.
- Stop offering the biscuit as a bribe during the shoe struggle. Food is given at fixed mealtimes only, never as a device to secure cooperation.
- Stop permitting the grandmother's Wednesday indulgence. Instruct her plainly that she is to give him whatever he wants no longer, and hold her to the same objective handling as the parents.

THE REGIMEN
1. Every morning, from to-morrow: Set out his shoes ten minutes before he need leave and let him work at putting them on unaided, wrong feet or no. Do not touch the shoes or his hands while he works.
2. The moment a hand is laid on the shoes or on him: Recognise that any hand laid on the shoes while he is working is what triggers the scream and the throw. Withdraw the hand and do not lay it on him again during the task.
3. Immediately, and every morning after: Do not restrain his hands or the shoes at any point in the struggle. If he cannot finish in time, he goes to nursery with the shoes as they are, or barefoot in slippers, rather than be restrained.
4. At once, permanently: Give up the practice of taking over the shoe task or moving him bodily from the counter. Substitute standing him at a low shelf of his own pans and spoons instead of pulling him away by hand.
5. Whenever dressing him at all: On the rare occasion you must dress him yourself, do it with smooth, unhurried movements and no gripping or jerking of the limbs.
6. 7.30 fixed, daily: Serve breakfast at 7.30 sharp every day, whether or not he has come downstairs on his own. Wake him in time to be at the table, rather than letting the meal wait on him.
7. One hour, after lunch, daily: Put him down for a full hour's nap after lunch every day without exception, not on roughly half the days as at present.
8. 5.30 p.m., daily: Move the tepid bath from 7.15 back to 5.30 p.m. sharp, held to every evening.
9. 7 p.m., daily: Move bedtime from about 8 p.m. back to 7 p.m. sharp, held firmly regardless of resistance.
10. In the bath-to-bed window, daily: Replace the father's rough play before bed with quiet occupation only - pencil, paper, or being read to - in the period between bath and bed.
11. Nightly, from to-morrow: Put him down awake at 7 p.m. and leave the room. Do not sit with him until he settles; let him fall asleep unassisted.
12. Ad hoc, to be eliminated at once: Withdraw the biscuit bribe entirely; offer no food outside the fixed mealtimes, whatever the morning struggle.

METHODS THAT WILL NOT WORK
- Explaining to him that you are late and reasoning with him about the shoes.
- Bribing him with a biscuit to secure cooperation.
- Putting the shoes on him while he is still half-asleep to avoid the struggle.

NOT COVERED
- Whether the child rages when moved from the counter or shows a separate, quieter behaviour there.
- Whether there is any fixed toilet routine at all.

EXPECTED COURSE
Expect the shoe-and-counter rages to worsen for two or three mornings once the household stops giving in, then to fall away sharply once no hampering or reward follows them; the over-conditioned dependence on cuddling will take longer, easing over some weeks of consistently objective handling. Establishing the orderly bedtime and the rest of the fixed schedule takes about a week of unremitting consistency before it holds of its own accord.

WATSON'S WORDS
Your boy of two and a half is not stubborn, nor was he born with a vicious temper. The morning shoe battle and the kitchen chase are nothing other than rage called out by daily restraint, kept alive by a household that rewards that rage by stepping in to finish his task, and answers all his crying with cuddling inside a schedule that is nowhere fixed. You and the other adults in your house have built this condition piece by piece, and the blame rests upon your shoulders, not upon the child.

Look at what you have actually done. When the child sets about putting on his shoes, he is engaged in an unpractised, clumsy motor habit. The moment you lay hands upon his shoes or his person to hurry him along, you hamper his movements. Hampering an infant's bodily freedom is the native stimulus that calls out rage. When he screams and throws the shoes, your household yields, takes up the task, and fastens them for him while he shrieks. You have attached a response to a stimulus and then rewarded the outburst with the very victory he sought. At the kitchen counter you repeat the blunder by seizing him bodily instead of directing him to an occupation of his own. By picking him up and soothing him whenever he cries, and sitting beside his bed until he sleeps, you have built an over-conditioned dependence upon bodily contact, made worse by meals that wander, a nap kept only half the time, and evening roughhousing that undoes whatever calm the day had left.

You will tell me, no doubt, that you do this out of kindness - that you want your boy happy and that you wish him to know he is loved. I ask you to examine your own heart more severely. Is it truly the boy's welfare you are serving, or is it your own emotional nature crying out for expression? When you pet him, carry him about, and hush his screams with your embrace, you are gratifying yourself, not building a man. Anything beyond a kiss on the forehead at good night, a handshake in the morning, and an occasional pat on the head for an extraordinarily good job serves you and damages the child. Mother love is a dangerous instrument. Unless you are willing to stifle a few sentimental pangs now, you will rear a boy unfitted for the world, forever demanding that others smooth his path and carry his burdens.

There are matters here on which my book does not speak, and I will not pretend to knowledge we do not possess. I cannot tell you whether the boy's conduct when moved from the counter is a separate, quieter habit or another display of rage, for your account does not make the facts plain; nor can I speak to his toilet routine, of which you have said nothing. Where the facts have not been gathered, behaviourism has nothing to offer, and I shall not guess.

In carrying out the regime I have set down for you, you must understand that it must run unbroken. Every adult in the household - father, mother, and grandmother alike - must be bound by the very same rule; a single lapse sets the training back days. You must expect the morning rages and the counter struggles to grow distinctly worse for two or three mornings once you cease your interference and your bribes. When the child finds that screaming no longer commands your hands, the display will drop away sharply. The appetite for perpetual cuddling will take longer, easing only over some weeks of cool, objective handling, while the fixed hours of sleep and rest will require a full week of unremitting regularity before they hold of their own accord.

Hold to the hours I have given you without flinching. If you do your part faithfully, you will have a child who never cries unless he is actually stuck by a pin; who loses himself completely in his own work and play; who overcomes his small difficulties without running to mother, father, or nurse for rescue; and who eats what is set before him and sleeps the moment he is laid in his bed.

The light was arranged so that we could show it either to the right or the left of the infant’s head. In order to keep the infant from turning its head, the experimenter held the head gently but firmly in his two hands. A soft cotton pad was placed on each side of the head so that the experimenter’s hands did not come into direct contact with the scalp. Even when very little pressure was exerted upon the head the infant began to cry and, if we continued to hold its head, it went into a real fit of rage. The same thing happens when we hold the feet or the legs together. In no case do we exert pressure enough to cause real pain. The response is first struggling, then crying. If the holding or hampering continues, the mouth opens wider and wider, the breath is held sometimes up to the point where not a sound can be heard, although the mouth is stretched to its fullest extent. 98 INFANT AND CHILD should not despair. The time was when we used to think it took generations to make a well-bred person. Now we know parents can do it in a few months’ time if they start to cultivate the garden before the weeds begin to grow. While no one can lay down a hard-and- fast routine of infant and child care which will fit every home, still certain general plans can be made and adhered to. Here are some suggestions for the two- to five-year-old child. Routine of Night- and Day-time Care The Bath: Unless counselled otherwise by your physician, 7 p.m. is a good bedtime for the ages two to five years. Before bed comes a tepid bath at 5.30 p.m. The bath should be a serious but not gloomy occasion. The object of the bath is to get the child clean and not to entertain it. Many mothers fill the tub full of celluloid toys and prolong the bath to a degree which is useless and foolish. The child cries when he has to get out—gets so interested in his water games that he never heeds your instructions in the art of washing and caring for himself. He should be taught as early as a year old to use a wash-cloth on himself, and at three and a half years of age he should be able to do most of the job alone. Of course, NIGHT. AND DAY-TIME CARE 99 from the beginning he must be handled gently and quietly, otherwise a slight accident, such as slipping under water, may condition him against his bath for a long time. The water in the tub should be not more than four to eight inches deep, depending upon the age of the child, and he should never be left in it alone until he has reached the age of six years at least. But don’t make the bath a nightmare by rough handling and carelessness. Situation: He is two and a half and he wants to put his own shoes on, but he takes ten minutes and gets them on the wrong feet. If I try to help he screams and throws them across the room. By then we are late for nursery so I end up doing it for him while he is screaming. This happens every single morning. He also follows me around the kitchen trying to grab things off the counter while I cook, and I keep having to move him away. I have tried explaining we are late, bribing him with a biscuit, and putting the shoes on before he is fully awake. Nothing has worked for more than a day.
Child's age: 2 years 6 months
Daily schedule: Up about 7, breakfast around 7.45 when he comes down. Nursery three mornings from 9 to 12. Lunch about 12.30. Nap is hit and miss, maybe half the days, around 1.30. Tea at 5.30. Bath about 7.15. Bed about 8, later if he fights it.
Who handles the child, and how: Mostly me. I pick him up and cuddle him when he cries, which is a lot in the mornings. My husband does bath and bedtime most nights and they play rough before bed. My mother has him on Wednesdays and gives him whatever he wants.
Sleeping arrangement: His own room, alone, door left open with the landing light on.
What the household does when he cries or rages: I pick him up and hold him until he stops. If we are late I do the shoes for him while he screams. At night one of us goes in and sits with him until he settles.
What has been tried: Explaining we are late, a biscuit if he lets me help, putting the shoes on before he is fully awake, and once leaving him to do it while I waited by the door. Nothing lasted more than a day.
Other children: None.
Anything sudden or frightening: No.
